content: Endometrial biopsy is a medical procedure in which a small tissue sample is taken from the lining of the uterus, known as the endometrium. This sample is then examined under a microscope to identify any abnormal cells or signs of cancer. The procedure can be performed with or without anesthesia. During the biopsy, the patient lies on their back with their feet placed in stirrups. The healthcare provider begins by performing a pelvic examination and inserting a speculum into the vagina to keep it open and visualize the cervix. The cervix is then cleaned with an antiseptic solution. To stabilize the uterus, an instrument called a tenaculum is used to gently grasp the cervix. If the cervical canal is narrow or stenotic, a cervical dilator may be used to widen it. A small, hollow plastic tube is then carefully inserted into the uterine cavity. Using gentle suction, a sample of the endometrial lining is removed. Once the sample is collected, the instruments are withdrawn. The tissue sample is sent to a pathologist, who examines it under a microscope for abnormalities. Endometrial biopsy is typically recommended for women experiencing certain symptoms or conditions. These include abnormal menstrual periods, such as heavy, prolonged, or irregular bleeding; postmenopausal bleeding; bleeding associated with hormone therapy; or a thickened uterine lining observed on ultrasound. The procedure is most commonly performed in women over the age of 35. It is also used to evaluate for endometrial cancer or precancerous changes (hyperplasia). In some cases, it is part of the diagnostic workup for infertility, as it can help determine whether the endometrial lining is responding appropriately to hormonal stimulation to support implantation of a fertilized egg. No special preparation is required for an endometrial biopsy. However, patients may choose to take an over-the-counter pain reliever, such as ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin IB) or acetaminophen (Tylenol), about one hour before the procedure to help reduce cramping. During the procedure, patients may notice that the instruments feel cold. Some discomfort or pain may occur when the cervix is grasped with the tenaculum. Cramping is also common as the instruments are inserted into the uterus and the tissue sample is collected. Potential complications of an endometrial biopsy are rare but may include infection, uterine perforation (creating a hole in the uterus), cervical tearing, prolonged bleeding, or light spotting. The results of the biopsy are categorized as either normal or abnormal. A normal result indicates that the cells in the sample show no abnormalities. Abnormal results may point to conditions such as endometrial cancer, precancerous changes (hyperplasia), uterine fibroids, uterine polyps, or hormonal imbalances. If the biopsy is performed as part of an infertility evaluation, the results may reveal whether the endometrial lining is being properly stimulated by hormones to support implantation. Other conditions that may be identified include abnormal bleeding related to tamoxifen use (a medication for breast cancer), anovulatory bleeding (bleeding without ovulation), or endometritis (inflammation of the uterine lining).
